title: Natural Materials
strapline: Conkers, pinecones, shells and sticks — free, beautiful and never the same twice.
intent: Handle materials with real sensory character — the weight of a pebble, the spiral of a shell, the spikes of a sweet-chestnut case — that no plastic resource can match.
Sort, group, count and pattern with objects worth caring about: all the conkers, the shells in size order, a pinecone-pebble-pinecone line.
Collect as curators: gathering treasures on walks, choosing what comes home, and owning a growing collection through the seasons.
Make transient art — mandalas, faces, tiny landscapes — where arranging is the art and nothing needs glue.
Read the seasons through the materials themselves: conkers mean autumn, catkins mean spring, and the basket changes with the year.
Respect where things come from — take fallen, not growing; leave the woodlouse's log as you found it.
implementation: Present collections beautifully — baskets, wooden bowls, a mirror or tuff spot base — because presentation tells children these things are precious.
Gather with the children, not for them: collecting bags on every walk, and a 'what did we find?' sort-out back at nursery.
Sit and arrange alongside, thinking aloud — 'I'm putting all my smooth ones together' — then leave space for children's own logic, which may be nothing like yours.
Count, compare and pattern in passing rather than as a task: conkers into the muffin tin, one each; whose stick is longest; what comes next in my line?
Photograph transient art before it's swept away, and display the photos — the making mattered, and the photos prove it.
Name the materials precisely — conker, acorn, cone, catkin, bark — children collect words as keenly as objects.
Model the collector's code every time: fallen things only, gentle hands for anything living, and put the log back the way you found it.
key_questions: How have you decided which ones go together?
Which is heaviest, do you think — how could we check?
What comes next in your pattern?
Where do you think this one came from?
How does it feel — smooth, spiky, bumpy?
What did we find in autumn that we can't find now?

impact.text: Children sort and group the collection by their own rules — all the shells, all the smooth ones — and re-sort when a new idea strikes.
Children make and extend patterns with cones, conkers and pebbles — and talk about what comes next.
Children count the things they've gathered because the collection matters to them — five conkers, one more than yesterday.
Children collect treasures on walks and talk about where each find came from.
Children link the basket to the seasons — conkers arrive in autumn, catkins in spring — and notice what the weather brings and takes away.
Children lift a log for woodlice, look gently and put it back — care for small lives becoming a matter of course.
Children arrange transient art with deliberate choices — this shell here, spiral facing up — and stand back proud of the result.
Children hold real back-and-forth conversations about their finds — where the shell might have come from, whose conker is champion.

enhancements: A mirror base or dark tuff spot under the mandala-making, doubling every arrangement.
Muffin tins and numbered bowls beside the conker basket — self-serve counting and one-to-one filling.
Balance scales with pebbles and cones — heavier-than guessing games that children can check themselves.
A seasonal shelf that visibly changes: conkers and crunchy leaves out, catkins and blossom in.
Magnifiers and a sorting tray for close looking — the spiral in the shell, the seeds in the cone.
Clay as a base for stick-and-stone sculpture when children want their arrangements to last.
A laminated 'collector's code' made with the children — fallen only, gentle hands, log goes back.

playing_exploring: Open-ended objects with no fixed purpose — a cone is an ice cream, a hedgehog, a rocket — invite exploration on the child's terms.
Every walk is a treasure hunt, and the finding is as rich as the playing.
active_learning: Balancing a pebble tower or completing a mandala ring takes patience children choose to spend.
Collections reward return visits — children pick up yesterday's sorting and take it further.
creating_thinking: Children impose their own order on the basket — categories, patterns, arrangements — and can explain their logic.
One object stands for many things across a morning; symbolic thinking with the cheapest resources there are.
